title: White House Launches 'Freedom Haulers' to Train Veterans as Truckers Amid Immigrant Driver Purge
summary: The roar of a big rig's engine might soon carry a new meaning: a second career for America's veterans. President Trump announced a major interagency effort Monday to steer former service members into trucking, capitalizing on a controversial crackdown that has sidelined tens of thousands of immigrant drivers. Since last summer, the Transportation Department has enforced long-dormant English language requirements for commercial drivers. The urgency intensified after an August 2025 crash in Florida, where a trucker from India performed an illegal U-turn, killing three. Secretary Sean Duffy declared that driver should never have been licensed. Subsequent audits across all 50 states uncovered widespread irregularities: non-domiciled CDLs issued without proper citizenship verification or remaining valid long after work permits expired. The result: approximately 26,000 drivers were removed for failing to demonstrate English proficiency, and 30,000 licenses were canceled as illegally issued. The federal government has threatened to withhold highway funds from states like California, New York, Pennsylvania, Minnesota, and North Carolina for noncompliance—battles now entangled in court. Enter 'Freedom Haulers.' The campaign promotes two pathways: veterans who recently operated military vehicles over 2.5 tons can waive the CDL skills test, while others can attend commercial driving school during their final six months of active duty, fully funded by the GI Bill—some even receiving a housing stipend. Over 40,000 veterans have already used the skills waiver. 'We are removing more and more dangerous foreign drivers off our roads every day and restoring the integrity of America's trucking industry,' Duffy said. 'Our new Freedom Haulers campaign will help build on these successes.' Werner Enterprises CEO Derek Leathers praised veterans' 'leadership, discipline and technical skills.' Yet immigrant advocacy groups argue the enforcement disproportionately targets Sikh drivers, citing the Florida crash and another fatal California incident. New rules further restrict CDL eligibility to specific visa holders (H-2A, H-2B, E-2), and require English-only testing—rules also facing legal challenges. With average trucker pay now at $70,000 and rates rising, the administration hopes the call of the open road will resonate with those who served.
why_it_matters: This story shows how a single accident can trigger a chain reaction that reshapes an entire industry. It highlights the trade-offs in public policy—improving road safety and creating veteran jobs versus protecting the livelihoods of longtime immigrant workers. For a generation that will enter the workforce soon, it's a real-world case study in how government actions can open some doors while closing others.

background_read: The U.S. trucking industry moves roughly 70% of all freight, making it a backbone of the economy. For years, a shortage of drivers led companies to hire immigrants, including many from India, often through special visa programs. An English proficiency rule for commercial drivers has been on the books for decades but was rarely enforced until recently.

Secretary Sean Duffy (appointed by President Trump to lead the Transportation Department) ordered sweeping audits after the 2025 Florida crash. Audits found widespread problems: licenses issued without verifying citizenship, and foreign-issued permits still valid after work permits expired. States that didn't cooperate—such as California, New York, Pennsylvania, Minnesota, and North Carolina—were threatened with losing federal highway money.

The GI Bill (the Servicemen's Readjustment Act, first passed in 1944) helps veterans pay for college, training, and housing. Using this benefit for trucking school is not new, but the 'Freedom Haulers' campaign gives it fresh focus. Werner Enterprises, one of the nation's largest truckload carriers, welcomed the push, citing veterans' discipline and technical skills.

Immigrant advocacy groups have pushed back, arguing the enforcement unfairly singles out Sikh drivers, who make up a significant portion of the trucking workforce. Legal challenges have been filed over both the English-only testing and the narrow list of visa types now eligible for commercial licenses.
Article_Structure: LEAD: Emotional opening—the rumble of a big rig as a symbol of a second career for veterans.
KEY POLICY: President Trump announces 'Freedom Haulers,' an interagency effort to steer veterans into trucking after a crackdown on immigrant drivers.
├─ TRIGGER: A fatal Florida crash in August 2025 by a driver from India, leading Secretary Duffy to demand audits.
└─ RESULTS: ~26,000 drivers removed for lack of English; 30,000 licenses canceled; federal pressure on noncompliant states.
THE CAMPAIGN DETAILS: Two pathways—skills waiver for those who operated heavy military vehicles, and fully funded CDL school via the GI Bill with possible housing stipend.
└─ STAT: Over 40,000 veterans have already used the skills waiver.
SUPPORT: Praised by Transportation Secretary Duffy and Werner Enterprises CEO Derek Leathers, focusing on safety and veteran qualities.
CRITICAL VOICE: Immigrant advocates say the enforcement disproportionately targets Sikhs. New visa restrictions and English-only testing face court battles.
CLOSING: Pay rising to $70,000, the administration hopes the open road will appeal to former service members—tying the policy back to the veterans' opportunity.

perspectives.perspective: Positive: A win for veterans and road safety
perspectives.description: Veterans gain access to stable, well-paying careers after service, and trucking companies get highly disciplined workers. Enforcing English proficiency can make roads safer, since drivers need to read road signs and communicate with law enforcement. The skills waiver also recognises the training veterans already have.

perspectives.perspective: Negative: Unfair targeting and economic harm
perspectives.description: Critics argue the crackdown disproportionately threw Sikh and other immigrant drivers out of work, even those with years of safe driving records. Removing tens of thousands of experienced drivers overnight could disrupt supply chains and raise prices. The new visa restrictions may also deny future immigrants a reliable path to a good job.

perspectives.perspective: Neutral: A pattern of using immigration rules to reshape the labour market
perspectives.description: Throughout history, the enforcement of licensing and language rules has sometimes followed economic anxiety or social tensions. In this case, a long-ignored regulation suddenly became a tool to reduce immigrant participation in trucking, echoing past moments when labour policy was used to favour one group over another.

perspectives.perspective: Forward-looking: Legal battles and a possible new model
perspectives.description: The lawsuits challenging English-only testing and visa limits could stall or reverse parts of the crackdown. If courts rule against the administration, many removed drivers might be reinstated. Looking ahead, the trucking industry might need broader solutions—like improving training for all aspiring drivers, not just veterans—to truly fix the long-term driver shortage.
